title: Distance, displacement, speed and velocity
learning_goals: Distinguish distance from displacement in words, diagrams and calculations.
Distinguish speed from velocity and include direction when stating a velocity.
Calculate average speed and average velocity for straight and two-dimensional journeys.
Recognise the exact information Cambridge expects in displacement and velocity definitions.

items.prompt: Which quantity needs a direction: distance or displacement?
A person walks away from a starting point and returns to it. Is the total distance zero?
items.answer: No. The displacement is zero, but the distance is the full path travelled.

items.prompt: Which quantity needs a direction: speed or velocity?

notes.title: How can one journey have two answers?
body: Maya walks from home to the library. Her fitness app says she walked 1.4 km, but her map says the library is only 900 m east of home.
Both measurements are correct. The app follows Maya's complete path. The map compares only where she started and where she finished.
Physics needs distance and displacement because one number cannot answer both questions.

notes.title: The path and the change in position

points: Total length of the path travelled.
Straight-line change in position from start to finish.
In one-dimensional motion, may be positive, negative or zero after choosing a positive direction.

notes.title: Precise definition
notes.accepted_meaning: distance moved in a straight line in a specified direction from a reference point
examiner_focus: Do not write only 'distance from a point'.

notes.title: Maya returns home
notes.prompt: Maya walks from home to the library and returns home by a different path. What happens to distance and displacement?
notes.answer: Distance keeps increasing. Displacement for the complete journey is 0 m because Maya's final position equals her starting position.

notes.title: Speed solves one problem - and creates another
notes.story: Two cyclists pass Maya at 10 m s⁻¹ in opposite directions. Their speeds are equal, but speed cannot describe which way either cyclist moves.

points: Tells you how fast an object moves.
Tells you how fast and in which direction the position changes.

notes.title: The missing information is direction
examiner_focus: A direction must accompany a numerical velocity unless the sign convention already gives it.

notes.title: Average values
notes.warning: Use totals. Total time includes time spent stationary. Do not average separate stage speeds unless the time intervals are equal.

notes.title: Worked example: Maya turns back
notes.scenario: Maya runs 300 m east from the school gate, notices that she dropped her phone, and runs 100 m west. The complete run takes 100 s.

steps.reason: Distance adds every part of the path.
Take east as positive, so west is negative.
Translate the positive sign into a direction.
Use total distance for average speed.
Use resultant displacement for average velocity.

notes.exam_link: Cambridge often uses a reversal to test whether the student separates total distance from resultant displacement.

items.mistake: Using total distance when calculating average velocity.
Giving a velocity as only 5.0 m s⁻¹.
items.fix: Add a direction, such as 5.0 m s⁻¹ east, unless a sign convention is stated.

items.mistake: Assuming distance and displacement must be different.
items.fix: They are equal in magnitude for motion in one straight direction without turning back.

items.mistake: Averaging two speeds by adding and dividing by two.
items.fix: Use total distance divided by total time unless equal-time conditions justify a simple mean.

notes.title: What to remember
items: Distance follows the path; displacement joins start to finish.
Speed uses distance; velocity uses displacement.
Average calculations use total distance or total displacement over total time.

practice.instructions: Attempt all questions without opening the solutions. Show working for calculations.

questions.prompt: Classify each quantity as scalar or vector: distance, displacement, speed, velocity.
marking_points: All four quantities classified correctly. Award 1 mark for each correct scalar pair and vector pair.

questions.answer: Distance in a straight line from the point in a specified direction.
marking_points: States straight-line distance/separation and includes direction.
States rate of change of displacement.

questions.prompt: A student walks 280 m along a straight path and then walks 80 m back along the same path. Determine (a) the total distance travelled and (b) the magnitude of the displacement.
marking_points: Total distance = 280 + 80 = 360 m.
Displacement magnitude = 280 - 80 = 200 m.

questions.prompt: A runner completes a 1.20 km route in 5.0 min. Calculate the average speed in m s⁻¹.
marking_points: Converts 1.20 km to 1200 m and 5.0 min to 300 s.
Average speed = 4.0 m s⁻¹.

questions.prompt: A train moves 2.4 km east in 180 s along a straight track. Calculate its average velocity.
marking_points: Average velocity magnitude = 13.3 m s⁻¹.
Direction stated as east.

questions.prompt: A shared e-scooter enters a zone with a speed limit of 20 km h⁻¹. Its display shows 6.0 m s⁻¹. State and explain whether it exceeds the limit.
questions.answer: Yes. 6.0 m s⁻¹ = 21.6 km h⁻¹, which is greater than 20 km h⁻¹.
marking_points: Correctly converts either value into the other unit.
Concludes that the scooter exceeds the limit.

questions.prompt: Figure 3 shows a cyclist following a curved route from X to Y. On the figure, draw and label (a) the distance travelled D and (b) the displacement S.
questions.answer: D follows the complete curved route from X to Y. S is a straight directed line from X to Y.
marking_points: Line D follows the curved path from X to Y.
Line S is a straight arrow from X to Y.

questions.prompt: A person walks 600 m north in 8.0 min and then 800 m east in 10.0 min. Calculate (a) the average speed and (b) the magnitude and direction of the average velocity for the complete journey.
marking_points: Total distance = 1400 m and total time = 1080 s.
Average speed = 1.30 m s⁻¹.
Resultant displacement = 1000 m.
Average velocity magnitude = 0.926 m s⁻¹.
Direction = 53.1° east of north, or an equivalent direction statement.

questions.prompt: A campus delivery robot travels from A to B, then from B to C, as shown in Figure 4. It moves 90 m east in 45 s and then 120 m north in 60 s. (a) Draw and label the resultant displacement R. (b) Calculate the total distance travelled. (c) Calculate the magnitude and direction of R. (d) Calculate the average speed. (e) Calculate the magnitude and direction of the average velocity.

answer.resultant_drawing: Straight arrow from A to C labelled R.

marking_points: Straight arrow from A to C labelled R.
Total distance = 90 + 120 = 210 m.
Uses Pythagoras to obtain displacement magnitude 150 m.
Direction = 53.1° north of east.
Total time = 105 s and average speed = 2.00 m s⁻¹.
Average velocity magnitude = 150 / 105 = 1.43 m s⁻¹.
Average velocity direction stated as 53.1° north of east.

exit_check.prompt: Which path quantity belongs in an average-velocity calculation?
When can distance and displacement have the same magnitude?
exit_check.answer: When motion is along one straight line in one direction without reversing.

exit_check.prompt: What information is missing from the statement 'velocity = 8.0 m s⁻¹'?
exit_check.answer: direction, unless a sign convention has already been defined

figures.purpose: Show route distance versus straight-line displacement in a familiar navigation context.
figures.description: Hand-drawn annotated teacher sketch of Maya walking from home to the library, with a winding coral path and a straight purple displacement arrow sharing the same endpoints.

figures.purpose: Show why a complete return journey can have non-zero distance and zero displacement.
figures.description: Hand-drawn annotated teacher sketch of Maya walking from home to the library and returning home by another route.

figures.purpose: Student annotation scaffold for distance and displacement.
figures.description: Simple black-line diagram with points X and Y and one smooth curved route joining them. Leave generous blank space around the route. Do not draw or label distance or displacement answers. Designed as an annotation scaffold.

figures.purpose: Student scaffold for the connected two-leg journey question.
figures.description: Clean right-angle route diagram. Point A at lower left, point B 90 m to the east, point C 120 m north of B. Show arrow A to B labelled 90 m east and arrow B to C labelled 120 m north. Do not draw the resultant A to C. Leave space for the student to add and label it.

figures.purpose: Create the need for velocity by showing equal speeds in opposite directions.
figures.description: Hand-drawn annotated teacher sketch of two cyclists passing Maya at 10 m s⁻¹ in opposite directions.

figures.purpose: Support the worked reversal journey without requiring two-dimensional trigonometry.
figures.description: Hand-drawn annotated teacher sketch of Maya running 300 m east and then 100 m west, with distance and displacement working.
